title.en: Tungnerdluk: The Child Taken by the Inlanders
title.zh: 通格內爾盧克：被內陸人奪走的孩子

region.en: Fiord winter-quarters and the inlanders' large house
region.zh: 峽灣冬居與內陸人的大屋

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; one manuscript plus a verbal narration, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Gathering berries with her only child, Tungnerdluk's wife turns away a moment and the inlanders have him. His father, guided by an angakok cousin, creeps hands and knees into the great house where two hags fight over the weeping boy — a huge helper sprung from the coast people hands the child over and warns of pursuit. Harpooning one pursuer from the beach, Tungnerdluk rows off; but the child sickens, and a second angakok, renowned at headlifting, flies to fetch the child's spirit back from the inlanders — restoring it, the baby recovers, and the mockers who come with whalebones are respectfully silenced by his storehouse.
summary.zh: 採莓時一轉身，通格內爾盧克夫人的獨子已被內陸人奪走。其父求教於巫師表親，獨自潛入大屋——兩個老嫗正為啼哭的孩子爭執不休；一名自稱源出海濱人的巨漢出手相助，把孩子交還並警告後有追兵。海灘上一叉刺翻一名追兵後，他們舉家出海；孩子卻病倒了——精於抬頭術的巫師飛往內陸，把孩子的靈魂帶回，嬰兒旋即康復。攜鯨骨前來嘲弄的訪客，在見識過他的鯨骨庫藏後悻悻而退。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note records an amarsiniook variant (monster of the inland ice) in which the falcon-tornak vanquishes the monster. Spirit-restoration (headlifting, angakok flight) documented as told.

passages.text: A man, whose name was Tungnerdluk, had his fixed abode by a firth, from which he made his regular excursions into the highlands to hunt the reindeer, and generally he was lucky; in winter he carried on seal-hunting at the mouth of the firth. One summer he was out chasing the deer as usual, and during his absence his wife went away to gather berries among the heather with their only child. She put the boy down on the sod and left him a moment; she had hardly turned away before she heard him crying out — although she instantly turned back, she did not find him in his place, but only heard his lamentations a long way off from where she was standing. She returned to the tent in great affliction, and told how she had suffered her child to be taken by the inlanders, adding that she feared her husband's anger. In the evening he returned heavily laden — 'I have got plenty of reindeer-flesh for thee' — and on finding that nobody answered, at once knew that some mischief had befallen them in his absence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He hurried in, and breathlessly asked if his son had died; the wife made no answer, but the others enlightened him: 'She let the inlanders take him.' Tungnerdluk asked his trembling wife to put new soles on his boots — he wanted to go and consult his cousin, who was an angakok. This man pointed out the place to which the boy had been taken, and accompanied the father on his way to find him. At a good distance they reached a large house, and the angakok told him he must go up to it alone, and that he himself would have to return. Tungnerdluk peeped in at the window, and saw two terrible women quarrelling and fighting about his weeping child; he leapt down into the outer passage, creeping on hands and feet to get through the inner one up into the main room. Having at last succeeded, he made his way up to the two hags to snatch his child — but whenever he tried to take it from one woman, she directly handed it to the other, and thus they went on a good while.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A huge man at length entered, who said he would assist him, declaring that he had sprung from the coast people: 'Thou'dst better run on beforehand: be sure I will soon come after with the child; but mind be quick — my house-fellows will soon be pursuing us.' Tungnerdluk came running at full speed and entered his tent, saying, 'Make ready to depart at once' — and meanwhile the other entered with the child. They folded their tents and quickly loaded their boat; at the very moment they pushed from shore they saw their enemies descending the hills. When they had fairly got down to the beach, Tungnerdluk could not resist putting back to fight them, and soon despatched one of them with his harpoon, then followed his own people out of the firth. After this his son fell sick, and he consulted an angakok who was not able to find out the cause; he then called another, renowned as a performer of headlifting, who conjured and called up spirits, lying down on his back, first letting go his breath, then rising up and beginning to breathe again, saying, 'The child's spirit is still with the inlanders.' 'Then lose no time in preparing for an angakok-flight to bring it back and restore it to us' — and he flew away to the inlanders, fetching the spirit of the child home with him. On his return to the parents he heard the voice of the child growing weaker; but by restoring the spirit to it the baby soon recovered. Tungnerdluk paid the angakok well with different kinds of victuals, adding, 'Whenever thou shouldst happen to be in any distress, I will gladly assist thee.' Shortly afterwards two visitors came on purpose to mock him, one carrying a lot of whalebones: 'We have heard of the celebrated Tungnerdluk, who fetched his child back from the inlanders; pray tell us some of thy achievements: we will make thee a present of our whalebones in return.' 'I am not in want of any such thing' — he took them to his storehouse, where he showed them his large stock of whalebones as well as of walrus-teeth; seeing this, they respectfully retired and left the place without so much as entering the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders'; not verbatim.

region.en: Akilinek, the fabulous country beyond the ocean

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; three tales under one number (North Greenland before 1830; southernmost Greenland c. 1860; author's verbal narration), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Three angakok-flight tales: a father initiates his son at the graves — hand thrust into the corpse's flesh, warned to flee at a spark falling from the setting sun — until the boy flies past his father's limit to Akilinek, where his iceberg-tornak séance is wrecked by a hairy woman's misstep, killing the house. The novice Ipisanguak finds the house of the bloody sword and exchanges places nightly with its dim-eyed angakok, until a topknot-ribboned girl with an anghiak wrecks his own iceberg séance and the Kagsimiut avenger is stoned back. A boy forced to sit on his conjuring father's knee hears stars dropping into the old grave, faints at the maggot-smell of its ghost, and wakes clairvoyant in the grave — to fly at last to Akilinek and share the wreck of a kivinngak iceberg that an anghiak turns upon the house.
summary.zh: 三則巫師飛行故事：父親在墓場為兒子行入門禮——手探屍身、囑其見落日滴下火花即逃——兒子終於飛越父親的界限抵達阿基利內克；降靈召來冰山靈，卻因毛婦失足而屋毀人亡。新手伊皮桑瓜克尋得『血劍之屋』，與其瞇眼巫師夜夜互換位置，直至繫彩帶、攜死胎鬼（安吉亞克）的少女令他的冰山降靈翻覆；復仇的巫師也被眾人擲石擊退。被父親按在膝上聽降神的小兒，眼見星辰落入古墓，嗅得蛆蟲之氣昏厥，醒來已在墓中、通曉千里——末了同往阿基利內克，又逢安吉亞克令冰山傾覆、全屋覆滅。

sensitivity.note: Documents angakok science: grave initiation, tornaks, headlifting, anghiak, kivinngak iceberg-tornak. House-destruction deaths recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: (1) There was once a very clever angakok. When he was about to practise his art, and his limbs had been tied and the lamps extinguished, he took flight, and having found the wind favourable, flew across the sea, but did not sight the opposite shore before daybreak, when he was obliged to return. Several times he tried to get farther away, but was never able to pass beyond this mark; and therefore he determined to educate his son for an angakok, hoping that he might possibly be brought to excel him. When the boy was grown up he went through all the grades and branches of the angakok-science; but when the father proposed to give up teaching him, the son turned very moody and low-spirited — 'Is there any part of the science thou thinkest we have overlooked, and neglected to practise?' 'I think there is.' After due meditation the father asked, 'Didst thou visit the graves?' — he had not — 'Well, I will take thee thither this evening.' At the burying-grounds the father opened one of the graves, undid the pall of a corpse beneath the waist, and made his son thrust his hand right into the flesh of the deceased body; this done, he left him as if nothing at all were the matter, remarking, 'As yet thou hast observed nothing particular at this tomb; but wait till thou seest the last rays of the setting sun, and take not thy eyes from its splendour: but the moment thou dost notice a spark of light falling down from it, beware, and flee the place at once.' While he stood gazing at the declining sun, the father suddenly beheld something glistening through the brightness of the sky, at the sight of which he immediately took flight — but the son remained with his hands attached to the corpse, unable to extricate himself. Not until midnight did he return, all smiles and joy; and now the father deemed him thoroughly tried and expert in his art.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the night of the following day he resolved to bind him for his first flight; when the lamps had been extinguished the son flew out, and having no particular end or aim, only went backwards and forwards, seeing nothing very remarkable — questioned concerning the currents of the air, he had not happened to take note of any. The next day he again prepared for an angakok flight, observing that the wind was favourable; he crossed part of the sea, and soon perceived that he was taking the same course as his father. At last great perpendicular rocks arose in front of him, and he had reached the limit of his father's journey; continuing his flight towards it and with some difficulty passing it, he saw an extensive country, crossed it in a southerly direction, and came upon a small house with two windows, alighting close beside it. Peeping within, he saw one man standing at each window, watching him closely; one of the men went out, beckoned to a woman, and invited the stranger to step inside. Seated on the side-ledge to the right, on the opposite side he saw a squint-eyed person whose breath was like fire (peculiar to angakut, and also only to be observed by them), bone-chips at his feet at which he had been working; further away a woman whose body was all over hairy. 'Why dost thou thus stare at me?' — 'Oh, I was only looking at the chips at thy feet.' — 'In the summer I have not got time to make chips, and that is why I am at it now.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of them said, 'Perhaps our visitor would like to show us some of his art?' — 'Why, I am not unwilling, though it is but the second time I have practised angakok science.' They all repaired to the kagse, their house of festivities; the squint-eyed person, always keeping close at the visitor's heels, asked him what fearful tornak he had got at his service — 'If I succeed, a large iceberg will presently appear.' They all entered the dark kagse, where he also observed the hairy woman, the sight of whom he did not like, suspecting her to be dangerous to his purpose. When the conjuring had begun and he felt that his tornak was drawing nigh, he said, 'I fancy that something is approaching us' — they looked out at the window and whispered, 'A monstrous iceberg is close upon the beach.' 'Let a young man and a maiden step forth and post themselves in the middle of the floor' — a tremendous noise proceeded from the iceberg bouncing ashore and suddenly calving; then a married couple was ordered out on the floor, and a loud roar from without followed; thus they were all called forth one after the other, and at last it was the turn of the ugly woman to step out — she missed her footing on one of the flags, got beyond the proper stepping-stones, and at the same time the iceberg turned over, came tumbling over the shore, and crushed the house to atoms. Only the angakok visitor and the man with the squint came out unhurt; tying his limbs, he rose high in the air and returned, accompanied by a swarm of croaking ravens. Silent and dejected — 'I am heavy with grief because I have practised my art badly: I did wrong in calling forth the hairy woman; and by this fault of mine many happy and vigorous people have perished.' Next day the squint-eyed person made his appearance: 'Perhaps I too may be allowed to exhibit my art? I too am an angakok.' 'My son there is just telling me that he has killed many brave and strong people by his want of experience.' 'So he did, the bad one.' Tied hand and foot, the squint-eyed began his flight in the house, and as soon as they began singing flew out of it; suspecting he might be dangerous, they extinguished the lamps to prevent his re-entering — but looking out at the window, they saw him take a direction towards his own homestead, and soon after proceeded to light the lamps, concluding that at any rate he would not return the same night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.

passages.text: (2) Of an angakok called Ipisanguak, who was still a novice in his art, this tale is told: On a certain evening, when he was just ready to set out on a flight, he said, 'I intend to go away in search of the little house my forefathers have often spoken of, outside of which lies the bloody sword.' Having spoken thus he set off, making a circuit all round the horizon without having anything particular to relate on his return; but the next time he flew straight across to Akilinek, and alighted right in front of a house where lay the bloody sword which was to be taken by him. A man emerged from the entrance whose eyes were all dim, like those of an unborn seal; he re-entered without noticing the stranger, and another man appeared whose eyes were like the blackest berries, asking him to step inside, the inmates welcoming him: 'Thou art just in time to join us at our meal.' After a while the angakok observed, 'I want another to fill my place at home to-night, otherwise my relatives will not believe that I have been here' — 'I should very much like to be thy substitute, but I am rather a slow one.' They proceeded to have him tied; presently he was lifted up within the house and soared out into the open air, while Ipisanguak enjoyed a happy night in the company of his pleasant hosts. At dawn of day he broke off — 'The night is done; I must be off' — and again crossed the sea; about midway he saw a glare as of a great fire shining about him, which appeared to be from his substitute, who likewise was on his way home, and thus meeting, both aimed at each other. Ipisanguak again visited Akilinek next evening, and at the same time his substitute exclaimed, 'I hear him coming; behold, there he is!' — and again they encountered each other on the way, smiled as they met, and returned in the same way at daybreak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the following day, when Ipisanguak returned from a trip in his kayak, he said he had met several kayakers from an adjoining place called Kagsimiut, and likewise reported that he had heard them say of himself, 'Ipisanguak has turned angakok, and almost every day exchanges place with an angakok from Akilinek. Let us go and hear him.' On the following day a great many kayakers and several boats' crews arrived; and when he suffered himself to be tied and left for Akilinek, he was soon replaced by his comrade, who entered the house and entertained the guests all the night long. Some time after this Ipisanguak paid a visit to Kagsimiut; during his stay one of the seal-hunters said, 'Seals are rather scanty with us at present: a clever hunter can hardly get one at a time; thou mightest bring on the seals, I should think, and thus improve the hunting.' At the same time Ipisanguak observed a handsome young woman, to whom he at once took a fancy, standing outside the house. In the evening he conjured spirits; during that interval an immense iceberg appeared fast approaching the beach — he now let the women advance one by one, but she to whom he had taken a liking would not come; at length one appeared with a fine new ribbon round her topknot, and at that very moment the iceberg began to waver and shake: the angakok immediately sank down beneath the floor and reached his own house by an underground way, while the iceberg came rolling on, tumbling right across the beach, crushing the house to atoms. On getting home he had all the lamps lighted; but in less than a moment the angakok from Kagsimiut made his appearance to avenge his people — they hit him with stones and drove him back, and his voice had become inaudible. The following day Ipisanguak went to have a look at the destroyed house, but not a trace was left of it. The girl with the new topknot was possessed of an anghiak (the ghost of an abortion, or a child born in concealment), and it was all owing to her that Ipisanguak had been the cause of the accident that had happened to her housemates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.

passages.text: (3) A great angakok at his conjurations always used to talk of his having been to Akilinek, and his auditors fully believed him. Once he forced his little son to attend his conjurations, sitting upon his knee; the boy, horribly frightened, said, 'Lo! what is it I see? The stars are dropping down in the old grave on yonder hill.' The father said, 'When the old grave is shining to thee, it will enlighten thy understanding.' Lying down in his lap for a while, the son again burst out, 'What is it I now see? — the bones in the old grave are beginning to join together.' The father only repeating his last words, the son grew obstinate and wanted to run away; but the father still kept hold of him. Lastly, the ghost from the grave came out, and being called upon by the angakok, entered the house to fetch the boy, who only perceived a strong smell of maggots, and then fainted away. On recovering his senses he found himself in the grave quite naked, and when he arose and looked about, his nature was totally altered — he found himself able at a sight to survey the whole country away to the farthest north, and nothing remained concealed from him; all the dwelling-places of man appeared to be close together, side by side, and on looking at the sea he saw his father's tracks stretching across to Akilinek. Going down to the house, he observed his clothes flying through the air, and had only to put forth his hands and feet to make them cover his body again; but on entering the house he looked exceedingly pale, because of the great angakok wisdom he had acquired down in the old grave. After having become an angakok himself, he once went on a flight to Akilinek, and entered a house where a number of men were assembled, one of whom he observed to be dim-eyed. By help of his angakok sense he discovered this man also to be an angakok, and remarked some bone-chips lying at his feet — probably supernatural ones, and only visible to a clairvoyant, which the dim-eyed man had in vain tried to get rid of, because they arose from some work he had taken in hand before the appointed days of mourning for some person deceased had gone by, thereby provoking the invisible rulers. While staying here, the angakok visitor was requested to make a conjuration in order to procure a plentiful seal-hunting: he summoned his tornak called a kivinngak — an iceberg, steep on one side but sloping down on the other, all covered with seals. The iceberg quickly approached with the latter side towards them, bending over, just about to cast off all the seals into the water — but it so happened that among the housemates who had stepped forth on the floor there was a woman with an anghiak, which immediately made the iceberg turn on its steep side; and tumbling over with a tremendous roar, it crushed the house and all the people within, all of whom perished excepting the two angakut, who took care to make their escape at the right moment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit
title.zh: 被惡意因格內爾舒特人俘虜的皮艇客

region.zh: 因格內爾舒特人的海濱巖窟

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; abridged variations of a popular theme, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Three captivity tales of the sea-shore gnomes: Kuvitsina's rock opens of itself, his kayak smashed, his nose cut off — until the tornak Napatarak severs his strings with 'What have ye been doing to Kuvitsina?' and the warning that earth-folk vanquish the very whales; his nose comes whirling home through the air to fit itself awry. Katauk, capsized without a bladder, is nose-cut and tied beneath the roof-beams — three tornaks relieve him, his killed erkungassok is breathed back to life, and the cut-up binding-thong becomes amulets for good kayakers. Ulajok is drawn by his own turning prow behind a white kayak into the lifted rock.
summary.zh: 三則海底精靈的擄俘故事：庫維茨納的巖石自動開合、皮艇被砸碎、鼻被割去——靈助納帕塔拉克喝問『你們對庫維茨納做了什麼？』替他解縛，並訓誡：『地上之人連我們所懼的鯨都能降服，你們更當敬畏他們。』他的鼻子飛旋歸位，只是稍有歪斜。無浮囊翻艇的卡塔烏克同遭割鼻縛樑；三靈助救他脫險，被殺的智靈被他呵氣復生；被割成小段的縛繩成了少年們習泳的護身符。烏拉約克的艇首自轉，被他身後的白艇一路引入升起的巖石之中。

sensitivity.note: Ingnersuit: gnomes of the sea-shore (Rink's Introduction). Nose-cutting and maiming recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: (1) Kuvitsina left the boat and the crew who had been his companions on their summer journey, whom he had followed down the firth, and in his lonely kayak went along the shore. As he approached a low steep rock, it opened of its own accord, and seeing this, he entered; no sooner had he got inside than he was surrounded by ingnersuit, who tore his kayak from him and smashed it to pieces. They took him away into the house, and put him down on the side-ledge, and their old housewife first sharpened her knife, went up to him, and cut off his nose, and tied him to one of the pillars. In this plight he at length bethought himself of his tornaks; the first he called, however, were not at all noticed by the ingnersuit, and had no effect upon them. It then occurred to him to call forth two tornaks he had amongst the benevolent ingnersuit; their approach was instantly heard, and one of them was named Nepingasuak, the other Napatarak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The latter of the two was the first to hasten to the spot, crying loudly, 'What have ye been doing to Kuvitsina?' He was in a terrible passion, and at once severed the strings, and further gave Kuvitsina an amulet, saying, 'Make haste, and be off!' — and he had thus escaped even before Nepingasuak arrived. On coming down to his ruined kayak, Nepingasuak merely breathed upon it, which soon made it all right; and thus he again returned to his own world, while Napatarak warned the ingnersuit, saying, 'Ye should never lay hand on the people who live on the face of the earth: ye ought much more to hold them in awe, because they can vanquish the beings we hold in fear, such as whales, which they catch by means of the bladder.' Kuvitsina had another name, which was Akamak. On his way home he met Nepingasuak, and at the same time observed a strange noise overhead: this was his nose, which came whirling along in the air, and adjusted itself in its proper place — only it became a little awry; and thus Kuvitsina reached his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.

passages.text: (2) Katauk, a very skilful hunter, used to catch seals by fastening the harpoon-line to his kayak without any hunting-bladder. Once, however, he happened to be capsized and drawn out of his kayak; being on the point of drowning, he gave himself up for lost, when all of a sudden he was surprised at the sound of kayakers approaching from the shore. He saw that they were the ingnersuit, and of the malignant sort; but still he thought it better to be captured by them than drown. He was carried off to their place, put down on the window-bench, and encouraged to talk — but seeing that he remained quite mute, they first cut off his nose, and then tied him up beneath the roof-beams. Being in the greatest distress he called his tornaks, three of whom instantly appeared and relieved him after a hard struggle; on going outside he found his erkungassok (the wise man among the tornaks) prostrate and killed, but quickly made him revive again by breathing on him. When he had pushed off in his kayak he heard a voice calling behind him, and a whistling besides; turning his face round, he beheld his nose, which came flying through the air, sent by his erkungassok; it soon fitted itself into its due place. In the evening, when he had gained his home, he felt a pain around his waist and loins, and looking at them, perceived one of the thongs with which he had been tied still attached; he cut it up in small bits, which he gave to young people for amulets, for the purpose of making them good kayakers. (3) Ulajok, while looking for seals outside the islands, came to a rock which was being washed by a heavy swell; at the same time he observed a bright kayak making great haste towards him — getting sight of Ulajok, the white kayak turned back and made for the rock again. Suspecting that he might be an ingnersuak, Ulajok wanted to turn his kayak homeward, but tried it in vain: the prow of his kayak always kept turning round, pointing anew at the rock, and insensibly he was drawn behind the white kayak. When close to the rock he saw it being lifted high up, and within, houses and people presented themselves; Ulajok was pulled to the shore, where the people put by his kayak and paddle, conducting him into a large house. (The rest of the story is much like the preceding two.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
